final_proof:
Let \(Q=\operatorname{pr}_{M,N}(P)\). We use the standard convention that the angle of a line through the origin is its inclination modulo \(\pi\). Thus, unless its inclination is \(\pi/2\), the line of inclination \(\alpha\) has equation \(Y=X\tan\alpha\); the line of inclination \(\pi/2\) is the \(y\)-axis.

First suppose that \(\theta=\pi/2\). Then \(M\) is the \(y\)-axis. Since \(M\ne N\), the line \(N\) is not vertical, so it has slope \(\tan\phi\). The line through \(P=(x,y)\) parallel to \(N\) therefore has equation
\[
Y-y=(X-x)\tan\phi.
\]
Setting \(X=0\) to intersect this line with \(M\) gives
\[
Q=(0,\,y-x\tan\phi).
\]

Next suppose that \(\phi=\pi/2\). Then \(N\) is vertical. Here \(\theta\ne\pi/2\), since otherwise \(M\) and \(N\) would both be the \(y\)-axis. The line through \(P\) parallel to \(N\) is \(X=x\), while \(M\) has equation \(Y=X\tan\theta\). Consequently, their intersection is
\[
Q=(x,\,x\tan\theta).
\]

It remains to consider the case in which neither \(\theta\) nor \(\phi\) equals \(\pi/2\). Put
\[
m=\tan\theta,\qquad n=\tan\phi.
\]
Then \(M\) and \(N\) have equations \(Y=mX\) and \(Y=nX\), respectively. Moreover, \(m\ne n\): equality would make these two equations define the same line, contrary to \(M\ne N\).

Write \(Q=(u,v)\). Since \(Q\) lies on \(M\),
\[
v=um.
\]
Since \(Q\) also lies on the line through \(P\) parallel to \(N\),
\[
v-y=n(u-x).
\]
This equation remains valid if \(P=Q\). Substitution of \(v=um\) gives
\[
u(m-n)=y-nx.
\]
Because \(m\ne n\), we may divide and obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
u
&=\frac{nx-y}{n-m}\\
&=\frac{x\tan\phi}{\tan\phi-\tan\theta}
 -\frac{y}{\tan\phi-\tan\theta}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Also \(v=um\), and hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
v
&=\frac{m(nx-y)}{n-m}\\
&=\frac{m(y-nx)}{m-n}\\
&=\frac{y\tan\theta}{\tan\theta-\tan\phi}
 -\frac{x\tan\theta\tan\phi}{\tan\theta-\tan\phi}.
\end{aligned}
\]
These are precisely the two coordinates in the third case.

Finally, each point just computed lies both on \(M\) and on the line through \(P\) parallel to \(N\). The intersection is unique: if the distinct origin-passing lines \(M\) and \(N\) had the same direction, they would coincide, so their directions are different. Therefore \(M\) meets every translate of \(N\) in exactly one point. Thus, in each case, the computed point is exactly \(\operatorname{pr}_{M,N}(P)\), proving the stated formula.
